screens.title: Logging and Monitoring with journald and rsyslog
screens.narratorSegment: Effective logging gives you the evidence you need when systems fail, services misbehave, or security incidents occur. In modern Linux, two complementary systems handle logs: journald, an integrated structured journal provided by systemd, and rsyslog, a long-standing syslog daemon that writes plain text files and forwards messages. In this lesson you will learn what makes journald faster and more queryable, when to enable persistent storage so logs survive reboots, and how rsyslog can consume journal output to produce the familiar /var/log files or forward logs to a central server. We will also cover practical disk-space controls: journal size limits and using logrotate for text logs. You will see concrete commands to inspect logs with journalctl, a sample logrotate configuration, and the common mistakes that cause lost data. By the end, you will know how to choose where logs live, how to query them precisely, and how to avoid a disk-filling logging system. Think about a recent incident you had: which log would you check first and why?

screens.title: What is journald?
screens.narratorSegment: Journald is systemd’s integrated logging daemon that stores messages in a structured, binary journal rather than plain text files. This structure includes metadata fields such as the originating unit, executable path, priority, and timestamps. The practical result is faster writes and powerful filtering: you can query logs by service unit, executable, time range, boot session, or severity with precision. For example, asking for all warning-level messages from the sshd service since yesterday returns exactly that slice, without scanning multiple text files. A concrete misconception to avoid is thinking binary means opaque: journald is queryable with journalctl, and tools read it just as reliably as text logs. Another misconception is that journald replaces plain-text storage; in many environments you still forward or export entries to rsyslog for archival or compliance. Key takeaway: journald gives you rich, searchable telemetry; learn its fields and query tools before assuming text logs are superior. How would this change your first step when investigating a failed service? What is journald? means journald stores structured, binary logs with metadata for powerful filtering and fast writes.. In practical terms, systemd's structured, binary logging daemon and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What is journald?

journald: structured journal

A system-level daemon that accepts messages from kernel, services, and stdout/stderr and stores them in a binary journal with metadata fields for precise queries.

Why structured logs?
  • Metadata fields let you filter by unit, executable, or boot session easily.
  • Binary storage is efficient and faster to write under load than many text files.
  • journalctl exposes rich queries without parsing text files manually.
Concrete example
Find warnings from sshd since yesterday: journalctl -u sshd.service --since "yesterday" -p warning
Misconception & takeaway
Binary does not mean unreadable or unusable. Use journalctl to extract human-readable slices. For archival or compatibility, forward entries to rsyslog or export text copies.
Key Takeaway

Learn journald fields and queries first; then decide when to export to text files for legacy tools.

screens.title: Using journalctl to query and follow logs
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl is the primary tool for reading the systemd journal. At its simplest, running journalctl shows entries from oldest to newest, but the real power lies in filters. You can follow live logs with journalctl -f, similar to tail -f. Filter by service unit with -u, for example journalctl -u sshd. service, or by time ranges with --since and --until, which accepts human-friendly strings like "2 hours ago". Use -p to limit output to a priority threshold; for instance -p err shows errors and above. Boot filters like -b and -b -1 let you inspect current and previous boots respectively. Combine filters to focus on precise slices, for example journalctl -u nginx. service -p warning -b -1 will show warning-or-higher messages from nginx during the previous boot. A common misconception is that journalctl is slow; when used with filters it reads the binary journal efficiently. Concrete example: to watch live kernel messages use journalctl -k -f. Practice combining unit, time, and priority filters and ask yourself: which combination would reveal a repeated failure pattern quickly? Using journalctl to query and follow logs means use -f, -u, -p, --since/--until, -k and -b to retrieve focused log slices for diagnosis.. In practical terms, essential commands and readable command examples for fast troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Using journalctl

journalctl commands

Readable command examples for common troubleshooting patterns.

Common commands
# Show all logs
journalctl

# Follow new entries
journalctl -f

# Show logs for sshd service
journalctl -u sshd.service

# Errors from last hour
journalctl -p err --since "1 hour ago"

# Previous boot warnings from nginx
journalctl -u nginx.service -p warning -b -1

# Kernel messages
journalctl -k
Tips, example & mistake
  • Combine filters to reduce noise rather than scanning large outputs.
  • Use -o short-iso for stable timestamp formats if you plan to script output parsing.
  • Misconception: relying on journalctl without persistence can lose logs after reboot. Enable persistent storage for investigations.
Key Takeaway

Practice combining -u, -p and time filters to answer specific incident questions quickly.

screens.title: Enable persistent journald storage
screens.narratorSegment: By default many distributions place journal storage in /run/log/journal which is volatile and cleared on reboot. In production you usually want persistence so logs survive reboots and power cycles. The process is simple: create /var/log/journal with appropriate permissions and restart the systemd-journald service. Concretely, run sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal and then sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald; journald will automatically switch to persistent storage under /var/log/journal/ when that directory exists. Verify with sudo journalctl --disk-usage to confirm storage location and space usage. A common mistake is creating the directory with restrictive permissions or forgetting to restart the daemon, which leaves logs in volatile storage. Another mistake is assuming persistence means unlimited growth: you should still set size controls in /etc/systemd/journald. conf. Example: after enabling persistence, trigger a few service logs and run journalctl -b to confirm entries persist across a reboot. Takeaway: persistence is a single directory creation and a restart, but always pair it with size limits to protect disk space. Enable persistent journald storage means create /var/log/journal and restart systemd-journald; then verify storage with journalctl --disk-usage.. In practical terms, make your journal survive reboots and verify the change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Enable persistent journald
Step-by-step
  1. Create directory: sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
  2. Restart journald: sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
  3. Verify: sudo journalctl --disk-usage and check /var/log/journal/
  4. Optionally generate logs and reboot to confirm persistence
Example
After creating the directory and restarting, run journalctl -b to confirm entries remain after a reboot.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to restart systemd-journald so the change does not take effect.
  • Not setting size limits, allowing the journal to consume all disk space.
  • Incorrect directory ownership or permissions preventing journald from writing.
Key Takeaway

Persistence is simple but incomplete without size controls; enable /var/log/journal and then configure limits in journald.conf.

screens.title: Configuring journald size and retention
screens.narratorSegment: Controlling journal size prevents logs from exhausting disk capacity. systemd-journald reads configuration from /etc/systemd/journald. conf where you can set directives such as SystemMaxUse which caps the total journal disk usage, and SystemKeepFree which reserves a minimum amount of free space on the file system. For example, SystemMaxUse=500M limits journald to roughly 500 megabytes. Another useful directive is RuntimeMaxUse which applies when the runtime directory is used. A common misunderstanding is to set very large limits and assume older entries are preserved indefinitely; journals are always subject to the configured limits and will rotate older entries out to stay within them. After changing journald. conf, restart systemd-journald to apply settings. Example: edit the config, set SystemMaxUse=500M, then sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald and run sudo journalctl --disk-usage to confirm the cap is seen. Takeaway: set realistic limits based on available disk space and retention requirements to balance forensic needs and system stability. Configuring journald size and retention means use systemmaxuse and systemkeepfree in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart journald to enforce disk usage limits.. In practical terms, control how much disk space the systemd journal can use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › journald size & retention
Key settings
SystemMaxUse: Caps total disk usage of persistent journal.
SystemKeepFree: Minimum free space to reserve on the filesystem.
RuntimeMaxUse: Cap when using runtime (volatile) storage.
Example change
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf
SystemMaxUse=500M
SystemKeepFree=1G
Misconception & verify
Do not assume a large cap preserves everything. Journald rotates older entries to respect limits. After editing, restart the service and verify with sudo journalctl --disk-usage.
Key Takeaway

Set caps that reflect retention needs and available disk space. Always verify with journalctl --disk-usage after restarting journald.

screens.title: What is rsyslog and how does it fit?
screens.narratorSegment: Rsyslog is a traditional syslog daemon that processes incoming log messages and writes them to plain text files, or forwards them to remote servers. Its configuration is typically located in /etc/rsyslog. conf and /etc/rsyslog. d/, where rules specify which facilities and priorities go to which destinations. For example, a rule like *. info;mail. none;authpriv. none;cron. none /var/log/messages sends informational messages except certain facilities to a common log file. In modern systemd systems, rsyslog commonly consumes messages from journald; journald can forward entries so rsyslog generates the familiar /var/log files or sends messages to a central syslog receiver. A common misconception is that rsyslog is obsolete—it's still critical for compatibility with older tools, plain-text archival, and network forwarding. Concrete example: configure rsyslog to forward auth logs to a remote server for centralized auditing. Takeaway: rsyslog remains a flexible bridge between structured journals and traditional file-based or networked logging architectures. What is rsyslog and how does it fit? means rsyslog writes plain text logs, applies facility/priority rules, and forwards logs to remote servers when needed.. In practical terms, traditional syslog daemon for file storage and forwarding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Rsyslog writes plain text logs, applies facility/priority rules, and forwards logs to remote servers when needed.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What is rsyslog?
How rsyslog works
  • Messages are matched by facility and priority and routed per rules to files or remote destinations.
  • Configuration lives in /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/ as rule statements.
  • Common destination: /var/log/messages and service-specific files under /var/log/.
Example rule
*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none /var/log/messages
Integration & takeaway
Use rsyslog when you need text-file compatibility, traditional rotation, or network forwarding. Pair it with journald forwarding for comprehensive coverage.
Key Takeaway

Rsyslog remains essential for archival, compatibility, and centralized logging; it complements journald rather than replacing it.

screens.title: How journald and rsyslog interoperate
screens.narratorSegment: In many modern setups journald and rsyslog work together: journald collects structured messages and can forward them to rsyslog, which then writes text files or forwards to a remote server. The forwarding path gives you two advantages: you retain journald’s query power while still producing plain-text archives and enabling centralized syslog collection. Practically, journald can be configured to forward messages using the ForwardToSyslog setting or via a socket rsyslog listens on. Once rsyslog receives entries, its familiar rules determine destinations. A common misconception is that forwarding duplicates statefulness; in reality, journald continues to manage its own retention and rsyslog manages its files separately, so you must configure retention policies on both sides. Concrete example: enable ForwardToSyslog in journald. conf, configure rsyslog to read from the journal socket, then check /var/log/messages to confirm entries appear. Takeaway: forwarding gives you best-of-both-worlds, but remember to manage retention and rotation on both journald and rsyslog to avoid disk surprises. How journald and rsyslog interoperate means forward journald to rsyslog to preserve queryability and also produce text archives or forward to central collectors; manage retention on both sides.. In practical terms, forwarding from journald to rsyslog for file storage or remote forwarding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Logrotate for plain-text logs
screens.narratorSegment: Logrotate automates rotating, compressing, and pruning old plain-text logs created by rsyslog or applications. A typical configuration lives in /etc/logrotate. d/ and describes the log path, rotation frequency, retention count, compression, and actions to run after rotation. For example, a my_app entry can rotate daily, keep three compressed archives, create the new file with specific ownership and permissions, and optionally restart a service in postrotate. A common mistake is failing to test configurations; use logrotate -d to debug and logrotate -f to force rotate for verification. Concrete example: create /etc/logrotate. d/my_app with a block specifying /var/log/my_app/app. log { daily rotate 3 compress missingok notifempty create 0640 root adm postrotate... endscript }. After forcing rotation, inspect /var/log/my_app to see app. log.1. gz and older files. Takeaway: logrotate is the reliable tool for text logs — write clear rotation rules, test them, and ensure any service that needs a file descriptor refresh is handled in postrotate. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › logrotate for app logs

Create a logrotate file

Sample configuration
/var/log/my_app/app.log {
    daily
    rotate 3
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 root adm
    postrotate
        # If the app needs a restart to reopen logs
        # systemctl restart my_app.service > /dev/null || true
    endscript
}
Testing & pitfalls
  • Test config parsing: sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/my_app
  • Force rotation for verification: sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/my_app
  • Common pitfall: not creating the directory or wrong permissions on the rotated files.
Key Takeaway

Write and test logrotate snippets for each custom log. Force rotations to confirm behavior before relying on automated runs.

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Two failure modes dominate logging problems: losing logs after a reboot and allowing logs to fill the disk. Losing logs commonly happens when persistence is not enabled and important events occur before an administrator can react. The fix is enabling /var/log/journal and confirming entries persist across reboots. Disk exhaustion often results from missing caps on journald or failing to rotate text logs generated by rsyslog or applications. For journald, set SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree in journald. conf. For text logs, write logrotate rules that compress and limit older files and test them with logrotate -d and -f. Another common mistake is assuming forwarding duplicates policies; forwarded logs live in two systems and both need retention policies. Example: creating a large SystemMaxUse without monitoring may preserve logs but still starve the root partition. Best practices: enable persistence, set conservative caps, configure logrotate for text logs, and test rotation and retention regularly. Takeaway: plan retention and test your configuration so logs remain useful and do not become a liability. Common mistakes and best practices means enable persistence, enforce size limits on both journal and text logs, and test logrotate and forwarding to avoid lost data or full disks.. In practical terms, avoid lost logs and disk exhaustion with sensible defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Effective logging gives you the evidence you need when systems fail, services misbehave, or security incidents occur. In modern Linux, two complementary systems handle logs: journald, an integrated structured journal provided by systemd, and rsyslog, a long-standing syslog daemon that writes plain text files and forwards messages. In this lesson you will learn what makes journald faster and more queryable, when to enable persistent storage so logs survive reboots, and how rsyslog can consume journal output to produce the familiar /var/log files or forward logs to a central server. We will also cover practical disk-space controls: journal size limits and using logrotate for text logs. You will see concrete commands to inspect logs with journalctl, a sample logrotate configuration, and the common mistakes that cause lost data. By the end, you will know how to choose where logs live, how to query them precisely, and how to avoid a disk-filling logging system. Think about a recent incident you had: which log would you check first and why?

Over this chapter you will master the essentials of Linux logging so you can diagnose problems reliably. First, you will learn the role and advantages of journald: how it collects structured, binary log data from kernel messages, services, and standard output, and why that structure makes queries faster and more precise. Second, you will become fluent with journalctl, using filters for units, time ranges, boot sessions, priorities, and executable sources so you can pull exactly the events you need. Third, you'll configure persistent journald storage and control journal size through systemd settings to protect disk capacity. Finally, you will understand rsyslog’s place in the stack: how to write simple rsyslog rules, forward logs, and integrate with journald. Each objective focuses on real commands and configuration steps used in production. As you work through hands-on steps, you will practice both reading logs and protecting disk space so logs remain useful and available when you need them.

Beyond understanding concepts, you'll perform practical tasks that reflect real sysadmin workflows. You will query specific services and time ranges so you can answer questions like: which SSH logins failed in the last hour, or which errors happened during the previous boot. You will enable persistent journald so an unexpected reboot does not erase forensic evidence. You will write a small rsyslog rule and verify messages land in /var/log/ files. Finally, you'll author and test a logrotate configuration for a custom application, forcing rotation and inspecting compressed archives. These are everyday operations for incident response, compliance audits, and capacity planning. A common misconception is that one system alone solves all needs: journald is powerful for search while rsyslog and logrotate are still needed for text-file compatibility and archival strategies. Practicing these tasks ensures you know which tool to reach for when time is critical.

Journald is systemd’s integrated logging daemon that stores messages in a structured, binary journal rather than plain text files. This structure includes metadata fields such as the originating unit, executable path, priority, and timestamps. The practical result is faster writes and powerful filtering: you can query logs by service unit, executable, time range, boot session, or severity with precision. For example, asking for all warning-level messages from the sshd service since yesterday returns exactly that slice, without scanning multiple text files. A concrete misconception to avoid is thinking binary means opaque: journald is queryable with journalctl, and tools read it just as reliably as text logs. Another misconception is that journald replaces plain-text storage; in many environments you still forward or export entries to rsyslog for archival or compliance. Key takeaway: journald gives you rich, searchable telemetry; learn its fields and query tools before assuming text logs are superior. How would this change your first step when investigating a failed service? What is journald? means journald stores structured, binary logs with metadata for powerful filtering and fast writes.. In practical terms, systemd's structured, binary logging daemon and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

journalctl is the primary tool for reading the systemd journal. At its simplest, running journalctl shows entries from oldest to newest, but the real power lies in filters. You can follow live logs with journalctl -f, similar to tail -f. Filter by service unit with -u, for example journalctl -u sshd. service, or by time ranges with --since and --until, which accepts human-friendly strings like "2 hours ago". Use -p to limit output to a priority threshold; for instance -p err shows errors and above. Boot filters like -b and -b -1 let you inspect current and previous boots respectively. Combine filters to focus on precise slices, for example journalctl -u nginx. service -p warning -b -1 will show warning-or-higher messages from nginx during the previous boot. A common misconception is that journalctl is slow; when used with filters it reads the binary journal efficiently. Concrete example: to watch live kernel messages use journalctl -k -f. Practice combining unit, time, and priority filters and ask yourself: which combination would reveal a repeated failure pattern quickly? Using journalctl to query and follow logs means use -f, -u, -p, --since/--until, -k and -b to retrieve focused log slices for diagnosis.. In practical terms, essential commands and readable command examples for fast troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

By default many distributions place journal storage in /run/log/journal which is volatile and cleared on reboot. In production you usually want persistence so logs survive reboots and power cycles. The process is simple: create /var/log/journal with appropriate permissions and restart the systemd-journald service. Concretely, run sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal and then sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald; journald will automatically switch to persistent storage under /var/log/journal/ when that directory exists. Verify with sudo journalctl --disk-usage to confirm storage location and space usage. A common mistake is creating the directory with restrictive permissions or forgetting to restart the daemon, which leaves logs in volatile storage. Another mistake is assuming persistence means unlimited growth: you should still set size controls in /etc/systemd/journald. conf. Example: after enabling persistence, trigger a few service logs and run journalctl -b to confirm entries persist across a reboot. Takeaway: persistence is a single directory creation and a restart, but always pair it with size limits to protect disk space. Enable persistent journald storage means create /var/log/journal and restart systemd-journald; then verify storage with journalctl --disk-usage.. In practical terms, make your journal survive reboots and verify the change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Controlling journal size prevents logs from exhausting disk capacity. systemd-journald reads configuration from /etc/systemd/journald. conf where you can set directives such as SystemMaxUse which caps the total journal disk usage, and SystemKeepFree which reserves a minimum amount of free space on the file system. For example, SystemMaxUse=500M limits journald to roughly 500 megabytes. Another useful directive is RuntimeMaxUse which applies when the runtime directory is used. A common misunderstanding is to set very large limits and assume older entries are preserved indefinitely; journals are always subject to the configured limits and will rotate older entries out to stay within them. After changing journald. conf, restart systemd-journald to apply settings. Example: edit the config, set SystemMaxUse=500M, then sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald and run sudo journalctl --disk-usage to confirm the cap is seen. Takeaway: set realistic limits based on available disk space and retention requirements to balance forensic needs and system stability. Configuring journald size and retention means use systemmaxuse and systemkeepfree in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart journald to enforce disk usage limits.. In practical terms, control how much disk space the systemd journal can use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rsyslog is a traditional syslog daemon that processes incoming log messages and writes them to plain text files, or forwards them to remote servers. Its configuration is typically located in /etc/rsyslog. conf and /etc/rsyslog. d/, where rules specify which facilities and priorities go to which destinations. For example, a rule like *. info;mail. none;authpriv. none;cron. none /var/log/messages sends informational messages except certain facilities to a common log file. In modern systemd systems, rsyslog commonly consumes messages from journald; journald can forward entries so rsyslog generates the familiar /var/log files or sends messages to a central syslog receiver. A common misconception is that rsyslog is obsolete—it's still critical for compatibility with older tools, plain-text archival, and network forwarding. Concrete example: configure rsyslog to forward auth logs to a remote server for centralized auditing. Takeaway: rsyslog remains a flexible bridge between structured journals and traditional file-based or networked logging architectures. What is rsyslog and how does it fit? means rsyslog writes plain text logs, applies facility/priority rules, and forwards logs to remote servers when needed.. In many modern setups journald and rsyslog work together: journald collects structured messages and can forward them to rsyslog, which then writes text files or forwards to a remote server. The forwarding path gives you two advantages: you retain journald’s query power while still producing plain-text archives and enabling centralized syslog collection. Practically, journald can be configured to forward messages using the ForwardToSyslog setting or via a socket rsyslog listens on. Once rsyslog receives entries, its familiar rules determine destinations. A common misconception is that forwarding duplicates statefulness; in reality, journald continues to manage its own retention and rsyslog manages its files separately, so you must configure retention policies on both sides. Concrete example: enable ForwardToSyslog in journald. conf, configure rsyslog to read from the journal socket, then check /var/log/messages to confirm entries appear. Takeaway: forwarding gives you best-of-both-worlds, but remember to manage retention and rotation on both journald and rsyslog to avoid disk surprises. Logrotate automates rotating, compressing, and pruning old plain-text logs created by rsyslog or applications. A typical configuration lives in /etc/logrotate. d/ and describes the log path, rotation frequency, retention count, compression, and actions to run after rotation. For example, a my_app entry can rotate daily, keep three compressed archives, create the new file with specific ownership and permissions, and optionally restart a service in postrotate. A common mistake is failing to test configurations; use logrotate -d to debug and logrotate -f to force rotate for verification. Two failure modes dominate logging problems: losing logs after a reboot and allowing logs to fill the disk. Losing logs commonly happens when persistence is not enabled and important events occur before an administrator can react. The fix is enabling /var/log/journal and confirming entries persist across reboots. Disk exhaustion often results from missing caps on journald or failing to rotate text logs generated by rsyslog or applications. For journald, set SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree in journald. conf. For text logs, write logrotate rules that compress and limit older files and test them with logrotate -d and -f. Another common mistake is assuming forwarding duplicates policies; forwarded logs live in two systems and both need retention policies. Example: creating a large SystemMaxUse without monitoring may preserve logs but still starve the root partition. Best practices: enable persistence, set conservative caps, configure logrotate for text logs, and test rotation and retention regularly. Takeaway: plan retention and test your configuration so logs remain useful and do not become a liability. Keep three practical ideas in mind. First, journald is systemd's structured, binary log store that provides metadata-rich messages and powerful filtering. Learn to use journalctl filters to extract relevant slices quickly. Second, rsyslog remains valuable for writing plain-text logs, applying facility/priority rules, and forwarding to central collectors; it complements journald, especially for archival and compatibility. Third, always plan for retention: enable persistent journald storage if you need logs across reboots, set size limits in journald. conf, and configure logrotate for text logs. A common operational trap is configuring only one side of the stack; forwarding requires retention policies on both journald and rsyslog. These actions form the operational core of log management: query, persist, and prune. When you face a live incident, pick the appropriate tool based on whether you need fast searchable data or a long-term plain-text archive, and ensure both sides have retention policies.
